Name: Mehrnaz Shoushtarian
Bio:
Biomedical Engineer with broad experience in research and development of medical devices used to measure neurological signals for monitoring medication effects or diagnostic purposes.
Experienced in regulatory processes for medical devices as well as establishing and working within ISO 9001 and ISO 13485 certified environments.

Name: Dan Polley
Bio: Dr. Daniel Polley holds the Amelia Peabody Chair in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery at Mass Eye and Ear. His research focuses on understanding the neural basis of sound perception, with a particular interest in disordered perception, difficulty understanding speech in noise, tinnitus (ringing of the ears), and hyperacusis. Basic research projects in the Polley Lab leverage recent advances in two-photon calcium imaging, multi-channel electrophysiology, deep brain imaging, and optogenetics to measure and manipulate neural circuits in awake, behaving mice. His clinically oriented research makes use of EEG, pupillometry, and psychophysics to develop new diagnostics and treatment strategies for “hidden” hearing disorders in human subjects. By studying the mechanisms and therapeutic potential of brain plasticity at the level of single cells all the way to clinical trials, the Polley Lab is pioneering new approaches to understand debilitating auditory perceptual disorders, for which there are no objective biomarkers, nor widely effective treatments.

Name: Christopher Cederroth
Bio: Christopher R. Cederroth is a biologist who obtained his PhD in 2009 at the University of Geneva (Switzerland). As a post-doc, he worked on hearing loss and tinnitus at the Rockefeller University and at the Karolinska Institutet, where he developed his pre-clinical and clinical research on hearing loss and tinnitus. In 2014, he obtains a faculty funded position at the Karolinska Institutet and creates the Laboratory of Translational Auditory Neurosciences. He obtains his "Docentur" in 2018 and becomes Associate Professor. In 2023, he joins the University Hospital of Tübingen where he aims at bridging animal and human research in order to elucidate the molecular mechanisms causing auditory neuropathy, hearing loss and tinnitus, develop new objective measures, and therapeutic approaches for their treatment. Since 2022, he is Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of the Association for Research in Otolaryngology.

Name: Hamid Djalilian
Bio: Hamid Djalilian, M.D. is board-certified and fellowship trained in Otology, Neurotology, and Skull Base Surgery. In addition to routine conditions of the ear, Dr. Djalilian’s areas of expertise include complex ear surgery, hearing loss, balance disorders, facial nerve paralysis, and skull base surgery. Dr. Djalilian is also a pioneer in the treatment of brain sensitivity disorders. These disorders present with a cluster of symptoms, such as tinnitus, headache, fatigue, brain fog, dizziness, vertigo, and chronic pain. Dr. Djalilian developed the highly successful Integrative Neurosensory Rehabilitation (INR) protocol for treating brain sensitivity disorders. The INR protocol is now used by many doctors and medical clinics across the country.

Name: Fan-Gang Zeng
Bio: Dr. Zeng's research focuses on diagnosis and treatment of hearing and speech disorders from auditory neuropathy and cochlear implants to tinnitus and hyperacusis.

Name: William Sedley
Bio: Dr Sedley runs a research group in Newcastle University investigating sensory processing mechanisms in the brain, especially related to the auditory system, and how changes in these processes can cause or contribute to clinical symptoms and conditions such as tinnitus, hyperacusis and migraine.

Name: Kelly Jahn
Bio: Research Interests: Improve treatments for hearing loss by studying how auditory perception changes across the lifespan and following acoustic injury

Name: Dirk De Ridder
Bio: Dr. De Ridder's research is centered on a Darwinian predictive brain model with Bayesian updating to adapt to an ever changing environment. This model is the basis to understand common pathophysiological mechanisms clustering groups of pathologies, such as thalamocortical dysrhythmias (pain, tinnitus, epilepsy, depression, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia) or obsessive compulsive spectrum disorder (addiction, OCD, eating disorders,...). This pathophysiological clustering permits to translate knowledge obtained from one disease to other diseases with similar underlying mechanisms, and to develop novel neuromodulation treatments based on it.

Name: Jinsheng Zhang
Bio: Jinsheng Zhang received a Ph.D. degree in auditory neurophysiology at University of Fribourg in Switzerland in 1997. He is a tenured full Professor in the Department of Otolaryngology, School of Medicine and the Department of Communication Sciences & Disorders, College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, Wayne State University. He is the Vice Chair for Research and Research Director of the Department of Otolaryngology at Wayne State University School of Medicine. He is the director of the Laboratories of Tinnitus and Auditory Neuroscience Research. His research interests encompass neural mechanisms underlying noise- and blast-induced tinnitus, tinnitus-related traumatic brain injury, brain neuromodulation with sound, electrical stimulation, light and pharmacological agents to treat tinnitus and related neurological disorders, multi-structure electrophysiological recordings, cross-modality neural plasticity, and auditory prostheses.

Name: Fatima Husain
Bio: Dr. Fatima Husain has degrees in computer science and cognitive neuroscience, with postdoctoral training at the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) on brain imaging and auditory neuroscience. Since 2008, the major focus of her research has been on tinnitus and hearing loss. She has published 24 peer-reviewed articles on tinnitus alone, with 22 of these focused on the use of brain imaging techniques to better understand the neural correlates of tinnitus and hearing loss, with a view to helping patients.

Name: Megan Beers Wood
Bio: Dr. Beers Wood combines her training in immunology with her postdocs in auditory neuroscience to study basic mechanisms of hearing. She is also passionate about teaching the creativity that science requires through mentoring. The Hearing Response Mechanisms through Observations of Neuro-Immunity in the Cochlea (HARMONIC) Laboratory, uses a combination of techniques including fluorescent imaging, flow cytometry, and deep neural network analysis of facial grimace and movement to understand how the immune system and neurons of the cochlea interact after exposure to loud noise. The long-term goal of Dr. Beers Wood’s research is to develop interventions to prevent or treat noise induced hearing loss (NIHL) or NIHL associated conditions such as pain hyperacusis.

Name: Julia Campbell
Bio: Julia Campbell received an Au.D in 2009 from the Department of Speech, Language and Hearing Sciences at the University of Colorado at Boulder. In 2015, she received a combined triple Ph.D in Speech, Language and Hearing Sciences, Behavioral Neuroscience, and Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Colorado at Boulder. Julia utilizes EEG methodology, ranging from single channel to high-density recordings, to investigate central auditory and visual processing in both children and adults. Source localization analyses are also a focus of her research, in order to view the cortical generators of EEG. Julia’s background in neuroscience research includes auditory cortical development in children with hearing loss, specifically using the cortical auditory evoked potential (CAEP) as a measure of age-appropriate development of the central auditory pathways. Her research has further examined visual cross-modal re-organization (recruitment of the auditory system by the visual system) as a result of auditory deprivation in both cochlear-implanted children and adults with mild hearing loss. In addition, she has investigated cortical changes in auditory processing in adults with mild hearing loss.

Name: Arnaud Noreña
Bio: Arnaud Noreña is a neuroscientist at Aix‑Marseille University whose work focuses on auditory perception, tinnitus mechanisms, and the neural plasticity underlying sound processing. His research integrates behavioral, physiological, and computational approaches to understand how the brain adapts to altered auditory input and how these changes contribute to hearing disorders

Name: Robin Cleveland
Bio: Robin Cleveland became the Director of the Institute of Biomedical Engineering in 2025. He is also a Professor of Engineering Science and Tutorial Fellow at Magdalen College, Oxford. He received his PhD in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin where his doctoral research was on sonic boom propagation in the atmosphere. Upon completion of his PhD he was award the F.V. Hunt Fellowship of the Acoustical Society of America which he carried out at the University of Washington in Seattle studying shock wave lithotripsy – breaking of kidney stones by shock waves. After two years in Seattle, Robin joined the faculty at Boston University where he remained for fourteen years rising to the rank of Professor of Mechanical Engineering. In 2011 he joined the University of Oxford, working in the BUBBL research group.

Name: Joel Berger
Bio: My primary research area is auditory neuroscience. I have a fascination with understanding how sound is represented within the brain, both in the presence of external stimuli and in the absence of an objective stimulus, as is the case with subjective tinnitus. As a musician, I have experienced first-hand the power that auditory stimuli can have on the brain. I am interested in furthering our understanding of basic neuroscience and translating this into benefits for patients, utilizing the latest tools in intracranial EEG, behavioral neuroscience, PET and source space EEG. My years of experience in Matlab analysis help me greatly in this endeavor.

Name: Robin Guillard
Bio: An engineer by training, then a neurotechnology entrepreneur, and today a passionate neuroscientist. My work lies at the interface of sleep medicine, auditory neuroscience, and translational research, with a particular interest in tinnitus, REM sleep, proteomics, and the functioning of the auditory system during sleep. Following entrepreneurial ventures in tinnitus (co-founder and CEO of two startups, managing teams of up to seven people) and receiving the Lopez-Loreta Prize (€1M), I fully committed to research to tackle the biological complexity of this pathology. My PhD thesis identified a subgroup of patients whose tinnitus fluctuates with sleep, specifically REM sleep. I am currently a postdoctoral fellow in Pr. Emmanuel Mignot's laboratory at Stanford University, where I work on biomarkers of sleep debt using large-scale proteomics data.

Name: Hui Hong
Bio: Hui (pronounced “Hway”) Hong is a neuroscientist specializing in the physiology, structure, gene expression, and function of the central auditory system. She obtained a B.S. in Biomedical Engineering from Tsinghua University in China and a Ph.D. in Communication Sciences and Disorders from Northwestern University. Following her doctoral studies, she completed postdoctoral training at Oregon Health & Science University under the mentorship of Dr. Laurence Trussell. In 2025, she joined the faculty at Creighton University School of Medicine as an assistant professor.

Name: Patrick Parker
Bio: Parker received his doctorate in neuroscience at the University of Utah, where he studied astrocyte management of glutamate signaling in a model of familial hemiplegic migraine. He is currently a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Dwight Bergles, Ph.D., in the Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Parker studies the brain effects of hearing loss, with a particular interest in spontaneous activity and changes in inhibition during sound processing. His expertise is in combining genetic and optical methods to explore brain physiology in living animal models. Parker’s 2026 Emerging Research Grant is generously funded by the Les Paul Foundation, and renewed for a second year in 2027.

Name: Inge Stegeman
Bio: Inge Stegeman studied Health Sciences at the Vrije University Amsterdam. She obtained her PhD in models for colorectal cancer screening in 2013, after which she was appointed as an epidemiologist at the Department of Otorhinolaryngology of the UMC Utrecht. Her research focus is on the quality of biomedical research with a focus on hearing and tinnitus.

Name: Sven Vanneste
Bio: Sven Vanneste is Chair of Clinical Neuroscience and Head of the School of Psychology at Trinity College Dublin. He is a Fellow of Trinity College Dublin and leads the Lab for Clinical & Integrative Neuroscience within the Trinity College Institute of Neuroscience. He is internationally recognised for research spanning systems neuroscience, clinical neuroscience, and neuromodulation. His work examines how large-scale brain networks generate perception, cognition, and persistent neurological and psychiatric symptoms, and how these networks can be modified to restore healthy functioning. Using electroencephalography, functional neuroimaging, computational modelling, behavioural methods, and invasive and non-invasive brain stimulation, his research focuses on tinnitus, chronic pain, memory, cognitive ageing, stress, fatigue, and predictive processing. A central goal is to advance precision neuroscience through objective biomarkers, clinically meaningful patient subtypes, and personalised neuromodulation treatments.

Name: Tom Naber
Bio: My research employs spatial transcriptomics in a tinnitus animal model to map gene expression landscapes within the auditory system, aiming to understand the molecular changes that contribute to tinnitus development. Some of my other research interests include neurotransmission of the cochlear inner hair cell synapse and the peripheral and central components of (hidden) hearing loss.

Name: Amy Conner
Bio: Post-Doctoral Fellow, Dpt Hearing & Speech Sciences, Vanderbilt University

Name: Kirupa Suthakar
Bio: Research interests: Neuroanatomy and neurophysiology of the descending auditory system, focusing on auditory efferent circuits, hearing loss, and non-canonical neuromodulation

Name: Junzhan Jing
Bio: Decipher the Building Blocks of Mouse Hippocampus CA1. Decipher Neuronal Types in Mouse Cochlear Nucleus. Identify "Seizure-Causing" Cell Type in Surgically Resected Tissue from Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy and Tuberous Sclerosis Patients. Von Economo Neurons in Monkey Anterior Insular Cortex. Microcircuit Deficiency in Single Gene Mutation Neurological Disorder

Name: Nicolas Gninenko
Bio: Nicolas Gninenko is a biomedical engineer at Neurosoft Bioelectronics developing ultra‑flexible neural interfaces designed to integrate seamlessly with delicate brain tissue. His work focuses on creating next‑generation implantable electrodes that improve signal fidelity, reduce inflammation, and enable long‑term monitoring or stimulation of neural circuits. He contributes to advancing soft bioelectronic technologies aimed at treating neurological disorders and expanding neuroprosthetic capabilities

Name: Kelly Assouly
Bio: Kelly Assouly is a Senior Research Engineer at Cochlear since November 2018 and a Post-doctorate Researcher at UMC Utrecht, also starting in November 2018. In addition, Kelly has served as a Media Promotion Coordinator at TRI Academy since July 2022. Prior experience includes a Master thesis conducted at the Translational Neural Engineering Lab at EPFL and engineering studies at Télécom Physique Strasbourg, where Kelly specialized in health information technology with a Master's degree in Micro and Nanoelectronics. Notable internships include work at AASDAP, focusing on brain interface machines and EMG data analysis, and at Inserm, contributing to neuroscience research on meditation's impact on emotion and auditory perception. Kelly possesses knowledge in various medical instrumentation, including EEG, MRI, and MEG.

Name: Jeremy Turner
Bio: Hearing Scientist and Professor with a special focus on preclinical animal models of hearing and the problem of noise, ultrasonic noise, and vibration in the vivarium.

Name: David Segar
Bio: I'm Dr. David Segar, a UCSF-trained functional neurosurgeon and the Medical Director at Nudge, where I serve as the principal investigator of a research study investigating low-intensity ultrasound neuromodulation for essential tremor. My work focuses on understanding the brain circuits involved in tremor and exploring how new technologies might help researchers study and interact with those circuits.

Name: Steve Barad
Bio: Steven Barad is a board member of Hyperacusis Research and an advocate for advancing scientific understanding of noise‑induced pain and sound intolerance. He works to connect patients, clinicians, and researchers, helping drive awareness, funding, and collaborative research aimed at uncovering mechanisms of hyperacusis and accelerating development of effective treatments.

Name: Yishane Lee
Bio: Yishane Lee is the Executive Director of the Hearing Health Foundation, where she leads national efforts to advance research, education, and advocacy for hearing loss, tinnitus, and related auditory disorders. She oversees the foundation’s Emerging Research Grants program, supports scientists working toward cures for hearing and balance conditions, and drives public outreach initiatives that promote prevention, early intervention, and equitable access to hearing health resources. Her leadership brings together researchers, clinicians, donors, and patient communities to accelerate scientific progress and expand awareness of hearing health.

Name: Kyleanne Hunter
Bio: Dr. Kyleanne Hunter serves as the Chief Executive Officer of Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), a role in which she provides strategic leadership to ensure the post-9/11 generation of veterans remains at the forefront of national conversations. A lifelong servant leader, Dr. Hunter is deeply committed to inspiring veterans to achieve their full potential and advocating for the policies necessary to support their journey.

Name: Jess Finucan
Bio: Highly decorated U.S. Air Force veteran with 20 years of experience, including 3 years of direct legislative liaison experience with the U.S. House of Representatives and extensive background in strategic communications, policy analysis, and program management. Proven ability to build relationships, advocate for organizational priorities, and navigate complex legislative processes. Expertise in defense and national security policy, coupled with strong leadership and communication skills.

Name: Russell Long
Bio: Russell Long is the founder of Long Capital, LLC and a committed supporter of scientific innovation in hearing health. He has provided meaningful financial backing to tinnitus research initiatives, helping accelerate work aimed at understanding the biological mechanisms of tinnitus and advancing potential therapeutic strategies. Through both philanthropy and advocacy, he contributes to expanding resources for researchers and strengthening efforts to develop effective treatments for chronic auditory disorders.

Name: Joe Sipos
Bio: Joe Sipos works in e-commerce at Amazon, focusing on consumer healthcare, where he has spent nearly seven years helping brands grow. Based in Austin, Texas, he is a former drummer who developed tinnitus and hyperacusis after an acoustic injury at age 30. He now advocates for better treatments and supports others, representing Tinnitus Quest at conferences and helping us gain exposure in the US.

Name: Jeffery Reagan
Bio: Jeff has lived with tinnitus since 2017. As both a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) and heart transplant recipient, he believes strongly in innovation driven by rigorous science and patient collaboration. Drawing on a career in information technology, Jeff advocates for integrating data science into tinnitus care. He founded the Tinnitus Learning Health Network™ (TLHN), which connects patients, clinicians, and researchers through shared data and insight.

Name: Hazel Goedhart
Bio: Hazel is a tinnitus sufferer who co-manages the Tinnitus Talk support community and the patient advocacy group Tinnitus Hub together with Markku Vesala, next to her day job at Morningstar, a financial services company, where she has held various leadership positions in research, product management, and customer success.

Name: Sven Köllmann
Bio: Sven has suffered from tinnitus since the age of 15. He is the CEO of FIBONA GmbH, and as an entrepreneur, he is used to solving difficult problems. He initiated Tinnitus Quest from a deep interest in medicine and science and a drive to change the lives of millions of tinnitus sufferers worldwide (including his own).

Name: Jack Rubinacci
Bio: Jack is a professional musician and songwriter, who has toured with and opened for a vast array of artists including Lionel Richie, Joe Cocker, Arcade Fire, The Script, Jackson Browne, The Chicks, White Lies, Heather Nova and more.He has had tinnitus for over 21 years and is volunteering huge amounts of time to support Tinnitus Quest’s PR efforts.

Name: Grace Pixton
Bio: Dr. Grace Pixton is an immunologist and protein engineer specializing in recombinant viral antigen design, pseudovirus and VLP assay development, and functional antibody characterization for emerging pathogens. She has been a tinnitus patient since 2024 when she experienced an inner ear barotrauma while SCUBA diving off the coast of southern California.

Name: Johan Fredriksson
Bio: I’m a high-agency generalist: I take initiative, learn quickly and bring people together to turn complex challenges into practical results. My work spans organisational development, project leadership, AI adoption and university administration. At Lund University, I combine admissions administration with staff development and practical AI adoption. I facilitate workshops, develop digital learning resources and lead the development of an online admissions course. I also conducted a needs assessment across all nine faculties and translated the findings into practical support. Alongside this, I founded Tinnitus Action, an independent initiative helping people take practical action to support progress towards better tinnitus treatments. I built the digital platform using AI-assisted development and lead its product development, content and action curation.

Name: Jennifer Svetlecic
Bio: https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/C5603AQFmtVUXtuqPag/profile-displayphoto-shrink_800_800/profile-displayphoto-shrink_800_800/0/1651266451089?e=1794441600&v=beta&t=j9v3AgW3an-YcKFjSNDc-AeDP8489-7tByeMkbtu4nM

Name: Amy Rommel
Bio: As Scientific Program Director at Rainwater Charitable Foundation, I help guide a portfolio aiming to find effective treatments for primary tauopathies. The work mostly supports the Tau Consortium, and additionally a few open RFAs and includes translational mechanisms, identifying potential drug discovery targets from early mechanistic research, biomarker discovery and validation, biobanks/registries, data platforms, and clinical trials—with adjacent work in glioblastoma, infectious disease (including Lyme), and tinnitus.
